title: Isaiah 53: 'my servant the Messiah,' says the Targum
claim: People often say that only Christians read Isaiah 53 as being about one individual Messiah. Classical Jewish sources say otherwise. Targum Jonathan, the official Aramaic paraphrase, opens the passage: 'Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper.' The Talmud asks what the Messiah's name is, and one answer cites Isaiah 53:4 — 'surely he has borne our griefs' (Sanhedrin 98b). Ruth Rabbah 5:6 applies Isaiah 53:5 to the Messiah's sufferings. An old Yom Kippur poem, preserved in Ashkenazi prayer books, speaks of 'our righteous anointed' who 'carries our sins.' The sixteenth-century commentator Moshe Alshich wrote that 'our rabbis with one voice' applied the passage to King Messiah. None of that proves Jesus is the Messiah. It does show that reading Isaiah 53 as one suffering individual is native to Jewish tradition, not a Christian import.
rabbinic: Yom Kippur Musaf piyyut 'Az milifnei bereshit'

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 3
Tovia Singer, 'Who is God's Suffering Servant?'

response: Rabbi Tovia Singer and Jews for Judaism answer that Christians quote these sources selectively. The Targum does apply the servant's exaltation to the Messiah. But it moves all the suffering onto Israel and the nations. Read whole, they say, it argues against a suffering Messiah rather than for one. Passages like Sanhedrin 98b are aggadah — homily and wordplay, not careful interpretation. Midrash regularly applies a verse to several different figures without settling its plain meaning. And the main medieval commentators — Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak — all read the servant as Israel. That fits Isaiah's own habit of calling Israel 'my servant' in Isaiah 41:8, Isaiah 44:1 and Isaiah 49:3. A tradition's sermons, they conclude, do not overturn its scholarship.
rationale: One narrow fact is agreed on all sides. Messianic readings of Isaiah 53 — including readings where the Messiah suffers — do exist in older Jewish literature. What is argued about is how much weight they carry, not whether they are there. So use the claim in exactly that form. Not 'the rabbis agree with us.' Instead: 'reading this chapter as one individual Messiah is a Jewish option, and it is an old one.' That is enough to move the conversation, and it is all the evidence supports. Overstating it hands Singer an easy correction, and he has a prepared one.

plain.d: Isaiah 53 is in the Old Testament. It describes a man God calls "my servant." He is hated. He is wounded. He is killed and buried. Then, somehow, he lives and is satisfied. Christians have pointed at this chapter for two thousand years.

plain.t: What your Jewish friend will say back
plain.d: That the servant is the nation of Israel, not one man. Israel suffered at the hands of other nations. So the chapter is about a people. This is the standard Jewish answer today, and it is a serious one.

plain.t: The part almost no Christian knows
plain.d: That answer became standard fairly late — after Rashi, a French rabbi, around 1100 AD. Before him, Jewish sources read the chapter as being about the Messiah. The clearest example is the Targum, the old Aramaic version that was read aloud in synagogues. It begins: "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper."
Very strong, because you are not using a Christian source. You are pointing at a Jewish one. Your friend can look it up without trusting you at all.

It changes what kind of conversation you are having. You are not telling a Jewish person what their own book means. You are asking a question about their own tradition. Those two things land completely differently.
"Have you ever read what the Targum says about Isaiah 53? I'd like to look at it with you."

title: The servant suffers for Israel, so he isn't Israel
claim: Inside the passage itself, the servant cannot simply be the nation. He suffers 'for the transgression of my people' (Isaiah 53:8). That makes the servant and the people two parties, not one. He is innocent — 'he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth' (Isaiah 53:9). Isaiah's Israel is not innocent, and Isaiah says so repeatedly, including in the same chapter: 'all we like sheep have gone astray.' The servant is silent under suffering (Isaiah 53:7), while Israel's laments fill whole books. He dies — 'cut off out of the land of the living,' given a grave — and yet afterwards 'prolongs his days.' The Hebrew Bible promises that Israel as a nation never dies (Jeremiah 31:35-37). And his suffering achieves something for others: 'he shall bear their iniquities' (Isaiah 53:11). Earlier songs already describe a servant with a mission to Israel (Isaiah 49:5-6).
rabbinic: Origen, Contra Celsum 1.55 (attesting the collective reading in the 3rd c.)

sources.name: Jews for Judaism, 'Isaiah 53 and the Suffering Servant'
Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 3

response: The strongest reply comes from Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Tovia Singer. Isaiah has already named the servant — 'Israel, my servant' — in Isaiah 41:8, Isaiah 44:1 and Isaiah 49:3. So the burden falls on anyone claiming an individual. Who is speaking in chapter 53? On this reading, the gentile kings of Isaiah 52:15, stunned at Israel's vindication. Each king says 'my people' about his own nation. That dissolves the servant-versus-people problem at 53:8. They also argue that the Hebrew preposition in 53:5 means Israel suffered from the sins of the nations, not for them. National Israel dying and reviving is standard prophetic imagery — Ezekiel 37's dry bones do the same thing. And this is not a medieval invention: Origen records Jewish opponents arguing it around 248 AD.

rationale: This one is graded Strong — meaning the Jewish counter-missionary answer does not deal with it properly. To make the collective reading work, you have to turn the gentile kings into the penitent confessors, and read 'my people' as meaning a different people in each king's mouth. Both readings strain the text. Isaiah 53:9 describes an individual grave, with 'a rich man in his death.' And the grammar of 53:5 runs the other way from the proposed reading: he was wounded for our transgressions, and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all. That is the language of one bearing what belongs to others. Still, say plainly that Isaiah does call Israel his servant elsewhere. If you skip that, you look like you are hiding it.

plain.d: If the servant in Isaiah 53 is the nation of Israel, the Christian reading of the chapter collapses. So everything turns on one question. Does the chapter treat the servant as the nation, or as someone separate from it?

plain.t: The verse that does the work
plain.d: Isaiah 53:8 says the servant was struck "for the transgression of my people." Read that slowly. The servant is punished for the people. So he cannot be the people. A nation cannot be punished for its own sins on its own behalf.

Isaiah 53:9 says he had "done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth." The prophets never say that about Israel. They say the opposite, over and over, at length. Isaiah himself does it in chapter 1.

plain.t: Where the other side has a point
plain.d: Isaiah does call Israel God's servant elsewhere — in Isaiah 41:8, Isaiah 44:1 and Isaiah 49:3. That is true, and you should say so first. The word "servant" alone proves nothing. The argument has to come from chapter 53 itself.

Strong for you. No Jewish answer deals with this properly. Counter-missionary writers — the Jewish teachers who answer Christian claims — usually move to Isaiah 41 and Isaiah 44 instead of facing verse 8 directly.

title: The Talmud's answer: two Messiahs, one killed
claim: The Hebrew Bible gives two pictures of the coming one, and they resist being merged. One is a reigning king from David's line (Isaiah 9:6-7, Jeremiah 23:5-6, Zechariah 9:9-10). The other is a figure who suffers, is pierced, and dies (Isaiah 53, Zechariah 12:10, Psalm 22, Daniel 9:26). Rabbinic Judaism saw both and answered with two Messiahs. Messiah son of Joseph fights and is killed — the Talmud applies the mourning of Zechariah 12 to his death (Sukkah 52a). Messiah son of David then reigns. Later midrash goes further: Pesikta Rabbati 36-37 describes a Messiah who accepts crushing suffering for Israel's sins. So the two-Messiah scheme is the tradition's own admission that both pictures are in the text. The Christian claim has the same shape and needs one figure instead of two: suffering servant first, returning king second (Luke 24:26).

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 2

response: The rabbinic answer is that Messiah son of Joseph is a warrior. He dies in the final battle against Gog. His death is not a sacrifice and accomplishes nothing redemptive. He also dies at the end of history, not centuries before the redemption. They add that the idea is post-biblical, marginal, and possibly a response to Bar Kokhba's death in 135 AD rather than ancient teaching. Above all, Maimonides' test stands. In the Mishneh Torah he says the Messiah is identified by what he achieves: a rebuilt Temple, the exiles gathered home, world peace, and everyone knowing God. Anyone who dies without doing those things is disqualified. Adding a second coming, they argue, is an unfalsifiable patch — and at least the rabbis' two Messiahs both act inside one redemption.
rationale: Here is what is conceded. The tradition itself found a Messiah who is killed, in these texts. Sukkah 52a hangs his death on Zechariah 12:10 — the same verse John 19:37 quotes. Daniel Boyarin, a professor of Talmud and not a Christian, argues that suffering-Messiah ideas are thoroughly Jewish. Use this to change what the conversation is about. The question was never whether Judaism could imagine a Messiah who dies. It plainly could, and did. The question is whether the one who died is the one who returns. That is a much smaller disagreement than most Christians and most Jews assume they are having.

plain.t: The problem sitting in the text
plain.d: The Old Testament seems to describe the coming one twice, in two ways that do not fit together. One is a king from David's family who wins and rules in peace. The other is a servant who is hated, pierced and killed. Both pictures are there.

This is not something Christians spotted. The Talmud — the huge Jewish collection of rabbinic teaching, finished around 500 AD — hits the same problem. Its answer, in a passage called Sukkah 52a, is two Messiahs. Messiah son of Joseph suffers and is killed. Messiah son of David reigns.
Less than it sounds. Not two people, but one person, twice. He came first as the servant. He returns as the king. Every piece of the rabbis' own solution is kept. Only the counting changes.
Very strong. The two-picture problem is admitted inside Judaism, in one of its own central books. You are not inventing the difficulty.
It stops the conversation being "my book versus your book." You are both looking at the same puzzle in the same text. You just solve it differently.
"Why is one person coming twice harder to believe than two different Messiahs?"

title: Daniel 9's order: anointed one dies, then Temple falls
claim: Daniel 9:24-27 sets out seventy 'weeks' for Israel and Jerusalem — a period to 'finish transgression' and 'bring in everlasting righteousness.' The part that carries the argument needs no precise arithmetic. Daniel 9:26 says an anointed one shall be 'cut off and have nothing,' and that afterwards the people of a coming ruler 'shall destroy the city and the sanctuary.' Whatever counting scheme you use, the anointed one is cut off before the destruction. That destruction happened in AD 70. So the window closed then. Strikingly, traditional Jewish chronology agrees about the end point: Seder Olam Rabbah runs the 490 years to the Second Temple's destruction, and Rashi identifies the cut-off anointed one with Agrippa at that same moment. Jesus was executed around AD 30, inside the last generation of the standing Temple. Josephus records that an 'ambiguous oracle' in the scriptures fed expectation that the time had come.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 1

response: There are two replies, and the second is much stronger. The traditional one: mashiach simply means an anointed person. Rashi reads the anointed one of verse 25 as Cyrus and the one in verse 26 as King Agrippa. The passage is about the Temple era, not a dying redeemer. The Talmud also curses those who calculate the end (Sanhedrin 97b), precisely because such maths produces false messiahs. The critical-scholarly reply is harder to answer. On that view Daniel 9 was written in the 160s BC. The anointed one 'cut off' is the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BC, and the destroyer is Antiochus IV. The seventy weeks then end in the Maccabean crisis. On this reading the Christian count depends on picking a convenient starting decree and treating symbolic sabbatical numbers as exact solar years.

responseSource.name: Sanhedrin 97b on Sefaria ("blasted be those who calculate the end")

rationale: Graded Contested — both sides have a real case. The Maccabean dating is the mainstream critical view and deserves to be named rather than ignored. But something usable survives every reading a Jewish friend is likely to hold. On the traditional Jewish chronology — Seder Olam and Rashi — the seventy weeks run out at 70 AD. So by the tradition's own arithmetic, whatever the passage is about, its clock stops at the destruction of the Temple. That is the version to use. Do not build an argument on a precise start date; you cannot defend it, and a prepared friend will know that.

plain.d: Almost any prophecy can be placed somewhere in history if you push hard enough. That is why arguing about them rarely settles anything. Daniel 9 is different. It puts events in a fixed order, and the last one has already happened.

Daniel 9:26 says an anointed one shall be "cut off, but not for himself." Then it says the people of a coming ruler shall "destroy the city and the sanctuary." The sanctuary is the Temple in Jerusalem. Rome burned it in AD 70.

The maths of Daniel's "seventy weeks" is genuinely argued about. There are several ways to count them and no agreement, even among Christians. Do not pretend there is. But the order does not depend on the maths. Cut off first. Temple destroyed second.
Contested, and say that. The order of events is strong. The date maths is not settled. Lead with the order and give away the maths before anyone asks.
It is the only prophecy here with a deadline that has already passed. That makes it checkable in a way the others are not — and Daniel is a book your friend already accepts.
"Daniel 9:26 has someone cut off before the Temple is destroyed. The Temple fell in AD 70. Who was that?"

title: A ruler from Bethlehem, foretold in the 700s BC
claim: Micah 5:2 reads: 'You, Bethlehem Ephrathah, little among the clans of Judah — from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient days.' That this verse is about the Messiah is not disputed between the two traditions. Targum Jonathan renders it 'from you shall come forth before Me the Messiah.' Rashi writes 'from you shall emerge for Me Messiah son of David.' The Gospels record the same thing as the standard Jewish answer to where the Messiah would be born (Matthew 2:4-6, John 7:42). Jesus's birth in Bethlehem is reported in both birth narratives, which are otherwise independent of each other. For Christian readers the phrase 'origins from of old' points past ancestry, and fits the child called 'mighty God' in Isaiah 9:6.
rabbinic: Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4 (Messiah and Bethlehem legend)

sources.name: Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah

response: The counter-missionary reading is that Micah names Bethlehem as the clan seat of David's family. 'From you' addresses the family stock — Ephrathah is David's clan, as in Ruth 4:11 and 1 Samuel 17:12. So the verse predicts a ruler descended from David, not a birthplace requirement. On that reading, 'origins from of old' means his family line reaches far back, not that he existed before he was born. They add that applying it to Jesus cannot be checked. The two birth accounts differ — Matthew has a flight to Egypt under Herod, Luke a census under Quirinius a decade later. The census mechanism itself is historically doubtful. And skeptics argue Bethlehem was written into the story because the prophecy was known.
rationale: The identification itself — that this verse is about the Messiah — is granted by the classical Jewish sources. That part is solid and worth establishing early, because it means both traditions agree that messianic prophecy with checkable content exists. What is genuinely contested is applying it to Jesus, which depends on the birth narratives, and on a reading of 'from everlasting' that the Hebrew does not force. Use the verse to establish the category. Do not use it as proof on its own.

plain.d: Micah wrote in the 700s BC. Micah 5:2 says a ruler over Israel will come out of Bethlehem Ephratah, and calls the town small — which it was. Then it adds that his "goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."
One is about a place: this ruler comes from Bethlehem. The other is about time: he existed before he was born. The first is simple and hard to argue with. The second is where all the disagreement is.

plain.t: What your friend will say back
plain.d: That the Hebrew phrase means an ancient family line, not existence from eternity. So the verse would be saying his ancestry goes back a long way — to David, and to Judah. That is a fair reading of the words, and the Hebrew can carry it.
Contested. The Bethlehem part is solid. The "from everlasting" part is a real translation debate. A Christian who pretends it is obvious will get corrected and lose the room.
Used gently it adds weight to the whole picture. Used as a knockout punch it hands your friend an easy win.
"How do you read the second half of Micah 5:2? I've heard it taken two ways."

title: Pierced in Zechariah, a slain Messiah in the Talmud
claim: Zechariah 12:10 says: 'They shall look to me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for an only son.' That switch — look to me, mourn for him — is in the Hebrew itself, not in the translation. The decisive piece comes from the Talmud. Sukkah 52a asks what the great mourning of Zechariah 12 is for. The accepted answer applies it to Messiah son of Joseph, who is slain, and quotes this very verse. So the classical Jewish reading closest to the plain sense already found a pierced, slain, mourned Messiah here. John 19:37 applies the verse to the crucifixion. The setting fits with unusual precision: the house of David and the people of Jerusalem looking in grief at one they pierced, with a fountain 'opened for sin' in the next verse.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 3

response: The strongest reply comes from Tovia Singer, Rashi and the NJPS translation. The speaker is God — 'they shall look to Me' — and God cannot be pierced. The Hebrew daqar here means slain in battle. So the verse describes national mourning at the end of history, over those who fell in the war of Gog and Magog. NJPS renders it 'they shall lament to Me about those who are slain.' The phrase 'et asher' can mean 'concerning him whom,' which removes the paradox of a pierced God entirely. Rashi does cite the Messiah son of Joseph tradition, but as aggadah about a warrior killed at history's end — not an atoning death under Rome. And some Hebrew manuscripts read 'look to him' rather than 'to me,' which takes away the Christian pivot altogether.

plain.d: Zechariah 12:10 describes a day when God pours out grace on Jerusalem. Then it says something strange: "they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him." The sentence starts with "me" and ends with "him."

plain.t: It is odd before anyone argues
plain.d: That shift is in the Hebrew itself. It is not a Christian translation trick. God is the one speaking, and yet the mourning is for someone else. Jewish commentators have wrestled with it for centuries.

plain.t: What Jewish sources make of it
plain.d: The strongest thing here is not a Christian reading. The Talmud connects this mourning to Messiah son of Joseph — the Messiah who is killed. That is the same figure from Sukkah 52a, and again it comes from inside Judaism.
Very strong, because you can make it entirely from Jewish sources. That is the only kind of argument that travels in this conversation.
A pierced figure, mourned by Jerusalem, read by Jewish sages as a Messiah who dies. That is a lot to set aside, and none of it depends on the New Testament.
"Why does Zechariah 12:10 switch from 'me' to 'him'? And what did the sages do with it?"

title: Psalm 22: one Hebrew letter, lion or pierced
claim: Psalm 22 reads like an eyewitness account of a crucifixion. It opens 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the words Jesus quoted (Matthew 27:46). Mockers shake their heads and say 'he trusted in the LORD, let him deliver him' (verses 7-8). 'They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots' (verse 18). And it ends not in death but in worldwide praise: 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD.' Verse 16 is the famous problem. The standard Hebrew text reads ka'ari — 'like a lion my hands and my feet,' with no verb at all. The pre-Christian Greek Septuagint reads 'they pierced my hands and feet.' And the Nahal Hever Psalms scroll, a Jewish manuscript from the first century AD, has the verb form. So the 'pierced' reading is ancient and Jewish. What it means is still debated.

sources.name: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library

response: They argue that ka'aru is not a known Hebrew verb for piercing. The root means 'dig,' and 'they dug my hands and my feet' is strained. The standard Hebrew — 'like a lion at my hands and feet' — fits the psalm's animal imagery, which already has bulls, dogs and lions. The psalm is David's own lament, written in the past tense, with no messianic label attached. Midrash Tehillim applies it to Esther. They also argue the Gospel writers shaped the passion account on the psalm, which would explain the fit. And one detail lands hard: the New Testament never quotes verse 16. If 'they pierced my hands and my feet' were decisive, the evangelists somehow missed it. Nothing in the psalm teaches atonement for others.
rationale: Graded Contested, and the honesty is the point here. The textual evidence — the Septuagint and the Nahal Hever fragment — genuinely supports an ancient verb here, and it refutes the charge that Christians invented the reading. But whether that verb means 'pierced' is uncertain, and the New Testament's silence about verse 16 is a real fact that an informed friend will raise. Concede it before they do. Then read the rest of the psalm, which needs no argument at all: the mocking in verses 7 and 8, and the clothing divided by lot in verse 18.

plain.d: Psalm 22 opens with the words Jesus quoted while dying: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" It goes on to describe a man surrounded by enemies, with his bones out of joint, mocked by watchers, and his clothing divided by lot. David wrote it centuries before crucifixion reached Judea.

Psalm 22:16 is the fight. The standard Hebrew text reads roughly "like a lion, my hands and my feet." The old Greek translation reads "they pierced my hands and my feet." One Hebrew letter separates the two, and the two letters look almost identical.

A scroll fragment found at Nahal Hever, near the Dead Sea, supports the "pierced" reading. It is about a thousand years older than the standard Hebrew text we normally use. That matters. But it is one fragment, and honest scholars still disagree.
Contested — and admitting that is the whole point here. A Christian who claims verse 16 obviously says "pierced" will be corrected, and will deserve it.
The rest of the psalm needs no argument at all. Psalm 22:7-8 has the mocking. Psalm 22:18 has the clothing divided and lots cast. Nobody disputes those verses. Give away verse 16 and read the rest.
"Let's set verse 16 aside — it's a real textual question. Read me Psalm 22:18."

refwhy.Psalm 22:1-31: The whole psalm. Read it start to finish. The parts that need no argument outnumber the one disputed word by a long way.
refwhy.Psalm 22:16(17): The contested verse, numbered 17 in Hebrew Bibles. This is the 'like a lion' or 'they pierced' problem, and it is genuinely unsettled.
refwhy.Psalm 22:18: 'They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.' Nobody disputes this verse. It is the one to read aloud.
refwhy.Matthew 27:35-46: Jesus quotes verse 1 from the cross, and soldiers divide his clothes. A Christian source, so give away verse 16 before you lean on it.
refwhy.John 19:23-24: Names Psalm 22:18 directly at the dividing of the clothes. The clearest New Testament use of this psalm, and it is not verse 16.
refwhy.Rashi on Psalm 22: Rashi reads the psalm as David's own lament, and takes verse 16 as 'like a lion.' The standard Jewish reading, and a reasonable one.
refwhy.Midrash Tehillim 22 (applied to Esther): An old Jewish commentary on Psalms that reads this psalm of Esther. Good evidence that Jewish tradition never fixed it on the Messiah.

titleLong: Psalm 22 — the crucifixion psalm and the kaari/kaaru textual question

title: Judah's rule expires when 'Shiloh' comes
claim: Jacob's blessing over Judah says: 'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples' (Genesis 49:10). Once again the messianic reading is native to Jewish tradition. Targum Onkelos renders it 'until the Messiah comes, whose is the kingdom.' Sanhedrin 98b lists 'Shiloh' among the Messiah's names. Rashi glosses it 'the King Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs.' So the Torah itself, read with rabbinic agreement, points to a specific individual at the end of Judah's line — one who commands the obedience not of Israel only but of 'the peoples,' plural. Christians add that Judah's remaining self-rule, the Sanhedrin's power over capital cases, lapsed under Rome in the generation before AD 70. Avodah Zarah 8b records capital cases ceasing 'forty years before the destruction.'

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 1

response: This answer has real teeth. If 'sceptre' means political sovereignty, it left Judah at the Babylonian exile in 586 BC, and stayed gone through Persian, Greek and Hasmonean rule — and the Hasmoneans were Levites, not Judahites. All of that is centuries before Jesus, so the popular 'it departed in AD 6' clock looks arbitrary. Rabbinic reading takes shevet as tribal identity and internal authority — the exilarchs, the patriarchs, the courts — which continued long after 70 AD. The phrase 'ad ki' can mean 'even when,' not 'until.' And 'Shiloh' itself is obscure: possibly the place name, possibly 'tribute to him.' Building a timetable on an uncertain word is unsound. The messianic reading in Targum Onkelos names the ultimate figure without conceding any first-century deadline.
rationale: This one splits in practice, so treat the halves differently. The messianic identification of Shiloh is conceded — Onkelos, Sanhedrin 98b and Rashi all make it, and those are common ground worth citing. But the popular Christian timing argument is contested and half-broken. The claim that the sceptre departed when the Sanhedrin lost the power of capital punishment ignores the Babylonian exile, which removed Judah's sovereignty far earlier. Use the identification. Drop the clock.

plain.d: Jacob is dying. He is blessing his twelve sons one by one. To Judah he says something odd. Genesis 49:10 keeps the ruler's staff with Judah "until Shiloh come." Then it adds: "unto him shall the gathering of the people be."

plain.t: Nobody is certain what Shiloh means
plain.d: Say that up front. It is one of the genuinely unclear words in the whole Old Testament. Suggested meanings include "the one it belongs to," a place name, and a title. Ancient Jewish translations read it as a name for the Messiah.

The verse ties Judah's ruling power to a deadline. So the question stops being about Hebrew and becomes about history: when did Judah's governing authority actually end? That is something the two of you can look up together.
Contested. The messianic reading is ancient and Jewish, which counts for a lot. The unclear word and the disputed history keep it from being settled.
It is one of the oldest passages Jewish readers treated as being about the Messiah. That was long before there was any argument with Christians about it.
"The Targum reads 'Shiloh' as the Messiah. What do you make of that?"

refwhy.Genesis 49:10: The verse. Jacob keeps the ruler's staff with Judah 'until Shiloh come.' Everything here hangs on one unclear word and one disputed date.
refwhy.Matthew 1:1-3: Traces Jesus to Judah through Perez. It matters only because the verse is about Judah's line, and this is the claim that he stands in it.
refwhy.Revelation 5:5: Calls Jesus 'the Lion of the tribe of Juda,' picking up Jacob's lion image one verse earlier. Christian use, not evidence.
refwhy.Targum Onkelos on Genesis 49:10: The Aramaic Torah version used in synagogues. It renders Shiloh as 'the Messiah, whose is the kingdom.' A Jewish source making the identification.
refwhy.Sanhedrin 98b: The Talmud page listing names for the Messiah. 'Shiloh' is one of them. Jewish, and long before any argument with Christians.
refwhy.Rashi on Genesis 49:10: Rashi glosses Shiloh as 'the King Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs.' The identification is common ground. The timing is not.
refwhy.Avodah Zarah 8b: The Talmud says the courts lost power over capital cases forty years before the Temple fell. Christians build a clock on it. Handle with care.

titleLong: Genesis 49:10 — the scepter of Judah and the one to whom obedience belongs

title: Don't open with Isaiah 7:14: 'almah' isn't 'virgin'
claim: Isaiah 7:14 says: 'The almah shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.' Matthew 1:23 quotes it for the virgin birth, using the Greek Septuagint's word parthenos. Here are the honest facts. Almah means a young woman of marrying age, as in Genesis 24:43 and Exodus 2:8. It is not the technical word for virgin, which is betulah. And the sign is given to King Ahaz with a short horizon — before the child knows good from evil, the two kings threatening him will be gone (Isaiah 7:15-16). Here is what Christians can still say. Jewish translators in Alexandria chose parthenos two centuries before Jesus, so that reading predates Christianity. The Immanuel child runs forward into Isaiah 8 and the divine child of Isaiah 9:6. And Matthew's word for 'fulfil' regularly means filling out a pattern, not bare prediction — he uses it the same way of Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15.
rabbinic: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 67 (Trypho's almah argument, 2nd c.)
response: This objection is ancient, and it is strong. Trypho was already making it to Justin Martyr around 160 AD. The Hebrew word is almah, a young woman. The sign is given to King Ahaz during a crisis in 734 BC, and it is useless to him if it happens seven centuries later. Verse 16 ties the child's early years to the fall of Rezin and Pekah. The child may well be Isaiah's own son — Isaiah 8:3-4 gives a boy with the identical timetable. They also note that parthenos in the Septuagint does not have to mean virgin technically: Dinah is called parthenos in Genesis 34:3 after she has been violated. So Matthew, reading Greek, built a doctrine on a translation choice. Later Jewish translators — Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion — rendered it 'young woman,' correcting rather than conspiring.

responseSource.name: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 43, 67 (New Advent)

rationale: Graded Don't use — this argument does not hold up, and saying so is this entry's main job. Isaiah 7:14 is not evidence for the virgin birth. It is Matthew thinking about a virgin birth he already believed for other reasons, using pattern-fulfilment — a normal Jewish reading technique of his day. Never open with this verse. Never present it as proof. Giving it away honestly is exactly what earns you a hearing on Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9, which do hold.

plain.d: Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." You have heard it read every December. It is also the weakest of the famous Christian proof-texts, and this page says so plainly.

The Hebrew word is almah. It means a young woman of marrying age. The specific Hebrew word for virgin is betulah, and Isaiah did not use it. So the English word "virgin" is carrying more weight than the Hebrew gives it.

Read the whole chapter. Isaiah is giving King Ahaz a sign about a war that was about to end. The child is a sign inside that crisis. A baby born seven hundred years later would not have helped Ahaz at all.

plain.t: What can still honestly be said
plain.d: Jewish translators — not Christians — rendered almah as parthenos, the Greek word for virgin, around 250 BC in the Septuagint. And Matthew is treating the verse as a pattern being filled out a second time, not as a one-meaning prediction.
Weak on its own. Use it as a pattern, or leave it alone. Giving this one away is exactly what earns you a hearing on Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9, which do hold.
"Honestly, I don't think this verse works the way it usually gets preached."

refwhy.Isaiah 7:14-16: Read all three verses, not just the first. Verse 16 ties the child's early years to two kings falling in Ahaz's own lifetime.
refwhy.Isaiah 8:8-10: Immanuel is named again here, inside the same crisis. Evidence that the child belongs to Isaiah's own century.
refwhy.Isaiah 9:6-7: The divine child of the next chapter. Any Christian case for reading Immanuel forward rests here, not on the word almah.
refwhy.Genesis 24:43: Rebekah is called an almah at the well. Shows the word means a young woman of marrying age. This one cuts against the Christian reading.
refwhy.Matthew 1:22-23: Matthew quotes the Greek version's 'virgin.' This is Matthew explaining a birth he already believed, not the reason he believed it.
refwhy.Matthew 2:15: Matthew calls Hosea 11:1 'fulfilled' by Jesus, though Hosea was writing about Israel. Proof that 'fulfil' here means filling out a pattern.
refwhy.Luke 1:34-35: Luke's account of the virgin birth never mentions Isaiah 7:14. Useful: the doctrine does not stand or fall with this verse.
refwhy.Rashi on Isaiah 7:14: Rashi reads the sign as a child born in Ahaz's own day. Strong for the Jewish side, and the chapter supports him.
refwhy.Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 67 (: A Christian record of a Jew making this exact objection around 160 AD. The objection is not modern, and it was never answered well.

titleLong: Isaiah 7:14 — almah, the Septuagint, and Matthew's typology (handle with care)

title: Before Jesus, a scroll: the Messiah raises the dead
claim: The charge that Christians read a Messiah back into neutral texts fails on pre-Christian evidence. The Dead Sea Scroll 4Q521, from the first century BC, says of the messianic age: 'the heavens and the earth will obey His Messiah… he will heal the badly wounded, he will revive the dead, he will proclaim good news to the poor.' That is strikingly close to how Jesus answers John the Baptist in Luke 7:22 — including raising the dead, which is not in the Isaiah passages underneath. Psalms of Solomon 17, from the mid first century BC, prays for the 'son of David' who will reign as 'Lord Messiah.' Qumran expected both priestly and royal anointed figures. Josephus records an 'ambiguous oracle' in the scriptures convincing many that a world ruler would arise from Judea in that era. The expectation was alive, textual, and clustered exactly in Jesus's generation.

sources.name: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library
John J. Collins, The Scepter and the Star
Craig Evans, Jesus and His Contemporaries

response: This one concedes the expectation, then turns it around. Yes, first-century Judea was full of messianic hope. That is precisely why there were so many claimants — Theudas, the Egyptian, later Bar Kokhba — and all of them failed the same test. The dominant expectation was a royal, national deliverer: Psalms of Solomon 17 describes a conquering king who purges Jerusalem of gentiles. As for 4Q521, it is fragmentary, and its wonder-worker may be describing God's own acts rather than the Messiah's. On this reading Jesus matched the minor motifs and failed the central ones. No throne. No exiles gathered. No peace. No rebuilt Temple. And the era's fever, as Sanhedrin 97b warns, is exactly what produced the false-messiah problem.

responseSource.name: 4Q521, Dead Sea Scrolls — text and translation

rationale: The conceded fact is powerful on its own. We have datable, pre-Christian, Jewish texts expecting an anointed one who heals, raises the dead and preaches good news to the poor. Luke 7:22 has Jesus answering John's question — 'are you the one?' — in exactly that vocabulary. Make 4Q521 the centrepiece. It cannot be a Christian forgery, because it was sealed in a cave before Jesus was born. That single fact removes the 'you invented it afterwards' objection permanently.

plain.d: A common claim is that Christians invented the Messiah they wanted, then read him backwards into the Old Testament. It sounds reasonable. It is also checkable, because we have Jewish writings from before Jesus was born.

plain.t: What the Dead Sea Scrolls show
plain.d: A scroll fragment called 4Q521 describes a Messiah under whom the blind see and the dead are raised. It is Jewish. It was written before Jesus. And it is almost word for word what Jesus later sends back to John the Baptist in Matthew 11:5.

The Psalms of Solomon, written roughly a century before Jesus, describe a king from David's line who cleanses Jerusalem and gathers the tribes. The expectation was alive, detailed, and datable. It was not made up afterwards.
Very strong. These are Jewish documents, dated by scholars who have no stake in the Christian conclusion.
It removes the "you invented it later" objection before it can be raised, using evidence that came out of a cave in 1947.
"Have you read 4Q521? It sounds a lot like Matthew 11, and it's older than Jesus."

refwhy.Isaiah 61:1-2: 'Good tidings unto the meek.' The Isaiah text underneath both the scroll and Jesus's answer to John. Read it to see what was expected.
refwhy.Isaiah 35:5-6: Blind eyes opened, lame men leaping. The other Isaiah passage behind that list. Note what is missing from both: raising the dead.
refwhy.Luke 7:18-23: John the Baptist asks 'art thou he?' Jesus answers with the scroll's own list, dead raised included. That extra item is the point.
refwhy.Matthew 11:2-6: The same exchange in Matthew. Cite whichever your friend has open. The wording that matters is the same in both.
refwhy.4Q521 (Messianic Apocalypse): A Dead Sea Scroll fragment older than Jesus. It says God's Messiah will heal, raise the dead and preach to the poor. Sealed in a cave.
refwhy.Psalms of Solomon 17:21-32: A Jewish poem from about 50 BC praying for the 'son of David' who will reign. Shows the royal hope was specific and datable.
refwhy.Josephus, War 6.312-313: The Jewish historian says an 'ambiguous oracle' in scripture made many expect a world ruler from Judea. A witness from the first century.

titleLong: Messianic expectation was alive, specific, and datable before Jesus — 4Q521 and Psalms of Solomon

title: The 'new covenant' is Jeremiah's phrase, not Paul's
claim: The phrase 'new covenant' — in Hebrew brit chadashah — is not a Christian invention. It appears in the Hebrew Bible, at Jeremiah 31:31-34. "Behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah — not like the covenant I made with their fathers, which they broke." Its content is spelled out: the Torah written on hearts, everyone knowing the LORD directly, and at the climax, 'I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more.' The promise assumes the covenant at Sinai could be broken, and was. It then announces a covenant built on final forgiveness. The New Testament stakes its whole self-understanding on this text: 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20), argued at length in Hebrews 8-10. Ezekiel 36:25-27 promises something parallel. Whatever you conclude about Jesus, the category belongs to Jeremiah, not to Paul.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 2

response: Read the content of the promise, they say. The new covenant is the same Torah — God says 'I will put my Torah within them' — written so deeply inside people that it can no longer be broken. Nothing here abolishes the commandments, replaces Israel, or mentions a mediator who dies. They also note that chadashah can mean renewed, the way the moon is renewed each month. And the timeframe is the messianic age, when 'they shall all know me' — which is plainly not the present world. Then comes their strongest move. The very next verses, Jeremiah 31:35-37, stake God's own reliability on Israel remaining a nation forever. That is the most powerful anti-replacement passage in the Bible, and it sits inside the passage Christians are quoting. If the church reads verses 31 to 34 literally, it must read 35 to 37 the same way.

responseSource.name: Jeremiah 31 with Rashi and Radak, Sefaria

rationale: Graded Strong — no Jewish answer deals with the narrow claim. The Hebrew Bible itself expects a new covenant, grounded in final forgiveness, promised to Israel. Christians did not invent the category — they claim it. But notice what the reply actually defeats. It defeats the overreach: that the Torah was abolished, or that Israel was replaced. Anyone using this entry has to renounce that overreach too, because Jeremiah 31:35-37 is in the same passage and says the opposite. So use it in both directions. It answers the charge that Christians made up a second covenant, and it rebukes any Christian who thinks God is finished with Israel.

plain.d: That Christianity invented a "new covenant" to replace the one God made with Israel. It gets said as though a new covenant were obviously a Christian idea, bolted on later to justify a new religion.

It is Jeremiah's. Jeremiah was a prophet in Jerusalem around 600 BC. He was writing to Jewish people. His book is part of the Hebrew Bible — what Christians call the Old Testament. So the phrase is not an import. It is already there.

plain.t: What the verse says, word for word
plain.d: Jeremiah 31:31 — "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." He names the two parties out loud: Israel and Judah. Not a replacement people. The same people God had made the first covenant with.

plain.t: And what this new covenant does
plain.d: Jeremiah 31:33 says God will "put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts." That means obedience from the inside, not rules imposed from outside. Jeremiah 31:34 says everyone will know God directly, "from the least of them unto the greatest." No middlemen. Then the last line, and the biggest one: God will "remember their sin no more." Not sin covered over. Sin forgotten.

Strong for the Christian side. There is nothing here for a Jewish friend to dispute, because the words are in their own Bible and they name their own people. The disagreement starts later, over who brought the covenant — not over whether one was promised.

It stops an argument before it starts. Say your friend claims Christians invented a second covenant. You are not defending a Christian idea. You are asking about a promise their own prophet made. He made it in their Scriptures. He made it to their people. The question is no longer whether a new covenant was coming. It is only who brought it.
"Who is Jeremiah's new covenant made with? Read me Jeremiah 31:31."

refwhy.Jeremiah 31:31-37: Read all seven verses, not the first four. Verses 31 to 34 promise a new covenant. Verses 35 to 37 promise Israel will never cease.
refwhy.Ezekiel 36:25-27: A parallel promise: clean water, a new heart, God's spirit within. Same idea, another prophet, also spoken to Israel.
refwhy.Luke 22:20: 'This cup is the new testament in my blood.' The moment Christianity claims Jeremiah's promise. That is a claim, not evidence.
refwhy.Hebrews 8:6-13: Quotes Jeremiah at length and says the first covenant is 'ready to vanish.' This is the overreach the Jewish reply rightly attacks.
refwhy.Rashi on Jeremiah 31:30: Hebrew Bibles number this verse 31:30. Rashi reads the promise as the same Torah, finally kept. No new law, and no new people.
refwhy.Radak on Jeremiah 31:30: Radak is David Kimhi, a commentator in Provence around 1200. He also reads renewal rather than replacement. Strong for the Jewish side.

titleLong: Jeremiah 31: the 'new covenant' is the Tanakh's own promise — made to Israel

title: For forty years, the crimson thread stayed red
claim: The Talmud records this: 'Forty years before the destruction of the Temple, the lot did not come up in the right hand; nor did the crimson-colored strap become white; nor did the westernmost lamp burn; and the doors of the Sanctuary opened by themselves' (Yoma 39b). The crimson thread turning white was the visible sign that the Day of Atonement had been accepted — the image comes from Isaiah 1:18, 'though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be white as snow.' The Temple fell in AD 70. Forty years earlier is about AD 30, the era of the crucifixion. On the Christian reading, the rabbis' own tradition remembers that from roughly the moment Jesus died, the signs of acceptance went dark, and stayed dark until the whole system ended. The same passage treats the failures as a mark of divine displeasure.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 1
Jacob Neusner, translations and studies of the Talmudic aggadah

response: They answer that this is aggadah — remembered homily, written down centuries after the events. 'Forty years' is the stock biblical and rabbinic number for a generation: the wilderness, Eli, David. The same tractate says the crimson thread had already been failing intermittently generations earlier, after Shimon HaTzaddik. And the rabbis give their own reason for God's favour being withdrawn, plainly and internally: the sins of that era, especially baseless hatred (Yoma 9b) and the corruption of the later priesthood. The passage never mentions the rejection of a messianic claimant. Building date-dependent theology on a symbolic number, against the text's own stated explanation, is exactly the proof-texting Jewish readers recognise in missionary material.
rationale: Graded Conceded, in the strict sense this section uses. The passage exists, it is Jewish, and it says what it says: the signs of divine acceptance failed for the Temple's last forty years, a span that lands around 30 AD. But carry the honesty with it. This is a suggestive convergence, not a proof. The number is schematic. And the passage supplies its own explanation, which is not the one Christians want. Present it as something striking worth explaining, and let your friend do the explaining.

plain.t: How the Day of Atonement worked
plain.d: Once a year the high priest drew lots between two goats. A crimson thread was said to turn white when the sacrifice was accepted. And a lamp in the Temple stayed lit as a sign that God was present. Everyone watched for those three signs.

A passage called Yoma 39b says that for the forty years before the Temple was destroyed, the signs stopped working. The lot no longer came up in the right hand. The thread stopped turning white. The westernmost lamp went out.
Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70. Forty years before that is AD 30. That is the traditional date of the crucifixion.
Very strong, and you never have to argue for it. This is not a Christian source. It is one of Judaism's own central books, describing its own Temple, and nobody disputes that the passage says this.
You do not have to make a case at all. You only have to ask someone to read it and tell you what they think happened in AD 30.
"Would you look up Yoma 39b with me? I'd genuinely like to know how you read it."

refwhy.Isaiah 1:18: 'Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.' The image behind the crimson thread the Talmud says stopped turning white.
refwhy.Leviticus 16:7-10: The Day of Atonement ritual: two goats, and lots drawn between them. Read it first, or the Talmud passage will not make sense.
refwhy.Zechariah 11:1: 'Open thy doors, O Lebanon.' The Talmud itself quotes this line about the Temple doors that opened by themselves.
refwhy.Matthew 27:50-51: The Temple veil torn at the death of Jesus. A Christian source, and the reason the forty-year detail interests Christians at all.
refwhy.Hebrews 9:11-12: Argues Christ entered the holy place once, with his own blood. The claim the Talmud passage is being used to support.
refwhy.Yoma 39b: The Talmud tractate on the Day of Atonement. It records that for forty years before the Temple fell, the signs of acceptance all failed.
refwhy.Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 6:3: The Jerusalem Talmud version of the same memory. A second Jewish record of the forty years, which is why it is worth citing.

titleLong: Yoma 39b: the Temple's signs failed for the forty years before the destruction

title: Atonement by blood, and no altar since AD 70
claim: Leviticus grounds forgiveness in blood offered in place of the sinner: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls' (Leviticus 17:11). The Day of Atonement worked by blood carried into the holy place (Leviticus 16). In AD 70 the altar vanished, and with it the entire system the Torah lays out — for nineteen centuries and counting. Rabbinic Judaism answered with repentance, prayer and charity. The Christian claim is that the timing is not an accident. Within one generation of Jesus's death — which the New Testament presents as the sacrifice the whole system pointed to, and which Isaiah 53:10 calls a guilt offering — God let the shadow end because the substance had come. Hosea 3:4-5 describes the shape of the age: many days without king and without sacrifice, before Israel returns and seeks 'David their king.'
rabbinic: Berakhot 26b (prayers instituted in place of sacrifices)

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 2
Jews for Judaism on atonement without sacrifice

response: This answer is substantial, and it is made from the Bible rather than around it. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly shows atonement without blood. A poor Israelite brings a flour sin-offering in Leviticus 5:11-13 — no blood at all — and 'the priest shall make atonement.' Hosea 14:2 prescribes the words of repentant lips instead of bulls. Solomon's dedication prayer in 1 Kings 8:46-50 anticipates forgiveness with no Temple, through repentant prayer. Daniel prayed without a Temple. Nineveh was forgiven for repentance alone in Jonah 3:10. Psalm 51:17 says the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. And Hosea 6:6 — 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' — was quoted by Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai after the Temple fell, and by Jesus in Matthew 9:13. Leviticus 17:11, they add, is about eating blood, not a monopoly on forgiveness.

responseSource.name: Leviticus 5:11-13 and Hosea 6:6 on Sefaria; Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4

rationale: Graded Contested — this counter-case is real Bible, not evasion. Flour offerings, Nineveh and Psalm 51 have to be conceded, and the claim that 'Judaism has no answer for sin' is simply false — this site should say so plainly. The genuinely open question is narrower, and worth asking carefully rather than triumphantly. The Torah's own centre of gravity for atonement is Yom Kippur, the altar and the blood. Judaism after 70 AD had to build a system without them. Asking where the Torah authorises that is a fair question. Claiming Judaism has nothing to say is not.

plain.t: What the law of Moses says
plain.d: Leviticus 17:11 is direct: "it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul." Atonement happens through blood placed on an altar. That altar stood in the Temple in Jerusalem, and nowhere else.
Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70. It has never been rebuilt. So the one thing Leviticus names as the means of atonement has been gone for nineteen centuries.

With prayer, repentance and acts of kindness. This is a serious answer, worked out by people facing a catastrophe, and it has carried Judaism for a very long time. Treat it with respect or the conversation is over.
The Torah names blood on an altar. The rabbinic answer names something else. So: where does the Torah authorise the replacement? Ask it gently, once, and then stop talking.
Contested. The question is real and hard. The Jewish answer is not stupid, and treating it as stupid will end the conversation on the spot.
"Leviticus 17:11 grounds atonement in blood on an altar. What grounds it now?"

refwhy.Leviticus 17:11: 'It is the blood that maketh an atonement.' The verse this case turns on. Note the Jewish reply: its subject is eating blood.
refwhy.Leviticus 16:29-34: The law fixing the Day of Atonement as a yearly statute for ever. Shows how central the altar was, which is what makes the question fair.
refwhy.Isaiah 53:10: Calls the servant's life 'an offering for sin.' The one Tanakh text that puts a person where the sacrifice stood.
refwhy.Hosea 3:4-5: Israel will go many days 'without a sacrifice,' then seek David their king. A Hebrew Bible text describing an age with no altar.
refwhy.Hebrews 9:22-28: 'Without shedding of blood is no remission.' The Christian argument stated, and also where it overreaches. Read it carefully before quoting it.

title: Why 'Judaism is all rules' died in 1977
claim: The caricature — Judaism as joyless rule-keeping to earn salvation, set against Christian grace — is false on the sources, and it destroys your credibility. The High Holy Day liturgy pleads Avinu Malkeinu — 'be gracious to us and answer us, for we have no deeds.' The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy from Exodus 34:6-7 anchor those days.
